title: More Than Enough: The Tabernacle's Curtains and Frames
summary: The craftsmen receive the people's gifts, but the offerings keep coming every morning until Moses has to tell the camp to stop giving. The workers then make the tabernacle's layers of curtains, its goat-hair tent and leather coverings, its gold-covered frames on silver bases, the crossbars, the veil woven with cherubim, and the embroidered curtain for the entrance.
story: Chapter 35 called for gifts and workers. Chapter 36 shows both at work. It opens with one of the most surprising scenes in the Bible: a people so eager to give that they must be told to stop. Only a few chapters earlier the same people had poured their gold into an idol. The building then begins where the plans of chapter 26 began, with the tent itself, the house God will live in, before the furniture in chapter 37 and the courtyard in chapter 38. Each detail repeats what God showed Moses on the mountain, now carried out in cloth, wood, silver, and gold.
historical:
The work takes place at Sinai during the months after the covenant renewal; according to 40:17 the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year. The structure described here is usually reconstructed as a rectangle about thirty cubits long and ten wide and high, roughly 45 by 15 by 15 feet (a cubit was about 18 inches, the length of a forearm), divided into a holy place and a smaller inner room, the Most Holy Place. The Hebrew word for the upright pieces (qeresh) may mean solid boards, but many interpreters think open frames are meant, since forty-eight solid planks of that size would be very heavy to carry through the wilderness.

Whether such a structure existed in the wilderness is debated, as the hard question below explains. What can be said is that portable, prefabricated sacred structures were known in the ancient world. From Egypt of the third millennium BC comes a dismantlable wooden canopy frame covered in gold, found in the tomb of Queen Hetepheres, and Egyptian reliefs of Ramesses II's military camp at Kadesh in the thirteenth century BC show a rectangular enclosure with the king's tent at its center, a layout Egyptologists have compared with the tabernacle and its courtyard.
cultural:
The tabernacle was built in layers of increasing value and holiness. The outermost coverings were leather and ram skins dyed red; under them was a tent of black goat hair; and innermost was the tabernacle proper, curtains of fine linen woven with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn and figures of cherubim. Priests standing inside would see the colored cherubim all around and above them. The same gradation runs from bronze in the courtyard to silver at the base of the walls to gold within. Every step inward was a step closer to God.

Cherubim in the ancient Near East were composite winged creatures, guardians of sacred space and thrones; similar figures flanked the thrones and palace doors of kings. In Genesis 3:24 cherubim guard the way back to Eden on its east side. The tabernacle also opened to the east (its rear was the west side, verse 27), and a veil embroidered with cherubim barred the way into the inner room. For Israel, God's house was a place where the way back to his presence was opened, but only through guarded and holy approach.
literary: The account turns command into fulfillment. In chapter 26 God said, you shall make; here the refrain is he made, with Bezalel the implied subject (37:1 names him). Verses 8 to 38 follow 26:1-37 closely, almost phrase for phrase, though the order of the whole section differs from the plans: the house is built before the ark and furniture, which came first in the instructions of chapter 25. The Greek Septuagint arranges and condenses these chapters differently from the Hebrew, a sign that they were copied in more than one form. The heavy repetition of numbers (fifty loops, fifty clasps, twenty frames, forty bases) gives the sense of exactness: nothing is left to guesswork, and nothing is invented by the builders.

doctrines.note: The whole structure is a house for a God who chooses to live among a people on the move. He is not tied to a fixed mountain or a single city; his dwelling travels with them. The care lavished on it expresses the worth of the one who lives there.

The layers of materials and the veil with cherubim teach that approaching God is a matter of degrees of holiness. God is near, in the middle of the camp, and yet not casually approachable. Both truths are built into the design.

The people's overflowing giving shows what a community looks like when it has been forgiven much: generous, eager, and needing to be restrained rather than pressured. The church has often read this scene as a picture of what grace does to giving.

words.note: Mishkan, tabernacle or dwelling place, from the verb shakan, to dwell or settle. It names the tent as the place where God lives among his people. Later Jewish writers used a related word, Shekinah, for God's dwelling presence, although that term does not appear in the Bible itself.

Keruv, cherub (plural cherubim). These are not the chubby infants of later European art but powerful winged guardians. They guard Eden in Genesis 3:24, overshadow the ark, and are woven into the curtains and veil here, making the tabernacle a picture of heaven's throne room on earth.

Paroket, the veil or inner curtain that separated the holy place from the Most Holy Place. Only the high priest passed through it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). It becomes central to the New Testament's language about access to God.

Day, sufficiency or enough. The craftsmen tell Moses that the people are bringing more than enough (verse 5), and verse 7 repeats that what they had was more than enough. The word marks a rare moment in Scripture when God's people give beyond what is needed.

christ: The New Testament sees the tabernacle's meaning fulfilled in Jesus. John writes that the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us (John 1:14), using a Greek verb related to the word for tent. When Jesus died, the veil of the temple, the successor to the one described here, was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). Hebrews explains the meaning: believers may enter the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way opened through the curtain, that is, through his body (Hebrews 10:19-20). Hebrews also describes the earthly sanctuary as a copy and shadow of the heavenly one (Hebrews 8:5). The veil with its guarding cherubim, which kept all but the high priest out, becomes in the New Testament the place where the way to God is opened.

hard.q: Could a structure like this really have been built and carried in the wilderness?
hard.a:
Scholars disagree. In the nineteenth century Julius Wellhausen argued that the tabernacle never existed and was a portable version of Solomon's temple projected back into the wilderness by priestly writers. Many critical scholars still hold some form of that view, pointing to the lavish materials and the close resemblance to the temple's plan.

Others argue for a real wilderness sanctuary. They point to the Egyptian parallels for gold-covered, dismantlable frameworks and for a royal tent at the center of a rectangular camp, both from the second or third millennium BC; to the wealth the Israelites carried from Egypt (12:35-36); and to the fact that the tabernacle's features fit a portable tent better than a stone temple. Some take a middle position: a simpler tent of meeting existed (compare 33:7-11), and the priestly description presents it in idealized detail. Readers who hold different views agree on what the text is teaching: God chose to dwell among his people, and he did so on his terms, in a house built to his design.

questions: The people had to be told to stop giving. What would have to change in you for generosity to become that eager?
Every layer of the tabernacle moved from common materials to precious ones as it moved closer to God. What does that suggest about how you approach him?
The veil kept people out, and the New Testament says Christ opened the way through it. How does access to God shape the way you pray?
